<header class="c-pagehead">
  <div class="c-wrap">
    <p class="c-eyebrow">Group · Molecular</p>
    <h1>Computational Biology</h1>
    <p>
      High-throughput biological data, read for mechanism — and carried forward.
      Our work spans the computational drug discovery pipeline: finding the
      disease signal in public omics data, testing with human genetics whether a
      target is causal, designing the molecule or biologic that engages it, and
      producing the safety and clinical evidence that decides whether it should
      be dosed.
    </p>
  </div>
</header>

<section class="c-slab c-slab--paper">

      <span class="c-eyebrow">Capabilities</span>
      <h2 class="c-h2">Six areas, one pipeline</h2>
      <p class="c-lede">
        The areas below are ordered the way a programme actually moves — a
        hypothesis becomes a target, a target becomes a molecule, a molecule
        becomes a dose, and a dose becomes evidence in patients. Projects
        usually sit in one area and borrow from the ones on either side.
      </p>
    </div>

    <div class="c-grid-3">
      <article class="c-card">

        <h3>Discovery Biology</h3>
        <ul class="c-rule-list">
          <li>Build consensus disease signatures across public omics datasets</li>
          <li>Cluster and annotate cell types in single-cell atlases</li>
          <li>Map spatial transcriptomics onto tissue architecture</li>
        </ul>
      </article>

      <article class="c-card">
        <span class="c-card-meta">Target validation</span>
        <h3>Human Genetics</h3>
        <ul class="c-rule-list">
          <li>Map GWAS loci to causal genes with fine-mapping and Mendelian randomisation</li>
          <li>Review tractability, druggability and tissue-specific safety</li>
          <li>Gate candidates on genetic constraint and direction of effect</li>
        </ul>
      </article>

      <article class="c-card">
        <span class="c-card-meta">Hit to lead</span>
        <h3>Medicinal Chemistry</h3>
        <ul class="c-rule-list">
          <li>Run large-scale virtual screens and triage the hits</li>
          <li>Design molecules generatively with synthesisable routes</li>
          <li>Predict ADMET properties and dock against the structure</li>
        </ul>
      </article>

      <article class="c-card">
        <span class="c-card-meta">Hit to lead</span>
        <h3>Protein Sciences &amp; Biologics</h3>
        <ul class="c-rule-list">
          <li>Predict protein structure and binding mode</li>
          <li>Design de novo binder and antibody candidates in silico</li>
          <li>Assess developability, immunogenicity and humanisation</li>
        </ul>

      <article class="c-card">

          <li>Model population PK and exposure-response to inform dose selection</li>
          <li>Predict off-target, hERG and secondary-pharmacology liabilities</li>
          <li>Detect adverse-event signals in public pharmacovigilance data</li>
        </ul>

        <ul class="c-rule-list">

<section class="c-slab c-slab--white">
  <div class="c-wrap">
    <div class="c-split">
      <div class="c-prose">

        <h2>Multi-omics integration in cancer</h2>
        <p>
          Genomics, transcriptomics, epigenomics, proteomics and metabolomics each
          describe one layer of a tumour. Integrated, they describe a system. We
          synthesise multi-dimensional data from international consortia — TCGA,
          GEO, ICGC — to characterise tumour heterogeneity and identify clinically
          actionable targets.
        </p>

        <h2>Bulk RNA sequencing</h2>
        <p>
          Bulk RNA-seq gives a high-resolution view of the transcriptome across a
          sample. We use it for differential expression, isoform discovery, gene
          fusion detection and alternative splicing analysis across pathological
          states.
        </p>

        <h2>Single-cell and spatial transcriptomics</h2>
        <p>
          scRNA-seq resolves expression to the individual cell, which is where the
          interesting heterogeneity usually lives. Our work here concerns the
          tumour microenvironment, rare cell populations, and the cell-state
          trajectories that accompany progression and immune response. Spatial
          assays put those states back on the tissue, so a signature can be read
          against the architecture it came from.
        </p>

        <h2>From target to molecule</h2>
        <p>
          Where a target emerges from the omics work, we ask whether human
          genetics supports it being causal — fine-mapping GWAS loci to genes,
          Mendelian randomisation for direction of effect, constraint and
          tissue-specific expression for safety. Targets that survive that gate
          are followed structurally, through binding-site characterisation,
          structure prediction, docking and stability assessment, and then into
          virtual screening, generative design against synthesisable routes, and
          in-silico binder and antibody design.
        </p>

        <h2>From molecule to dose and evidence</h2>
        <p>
          A candidate is only useful at a dose that works and does not harm. We
          model population PK and exposure-response to inform dose selection,
          predict off-target, hERG and secondary-pharmacology liabilities, and
          mine public pharmacovigilance data for adverse-event signals.
          Downstream, real-world EHR and claims data, survival analysis and
          systematic meta-analysis test whether the effect holds in patients.
        </p>

        <h2>Selected outputs</h2>
        <p>
          <a href="../../publications/">Pan-cancer analysis reveals immunological and prognostic significance of CCT5 in human tumors</a>,
          <em>Scientific Reports</em>, 2025.
        </p>
